sec.title: Background
sec.p: T-cell immunoglobulin and mucin-domain containing 3 (TIM-3) is an inhibitory receptor linked to decreased antitumor activity of immune cells. S095018 is a human anti-TIM-3 IgG2 antibody that blocks the binding of phosphatidyl serine to TIM-3. Sym021 is a humanized IgG1 antibody that inhibits the binding of programmed cell death protein-1 (PD-1) to its ligands programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) and PD-L2.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: S095018 in combination with Sym021 was tested in patients with advanced/metastatic biliary tract cancers (BTC) whose disease progressed under treatment with at least 1 line of systemic therapy and who had not received prior treatment with PD-(L)1 inhibitors (NCT04641871). Patients received 3 mg/kg of Sym021 and 10 mg/kg of S095018 once every 2 weeks. Primary endpoints included overall response rate and incidence/severity of adverse events. Key secondary endpoints included pharmacokinetics, immunogenicity assessment, progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS).

sec.title: Results
sec.p: 35 patients with stage IV BTC received S095018 in combination with Sym021. A partial response was achieved in 2 patients (5.7%) and stable disease in 11 patients (31.4%) for a disease control rate of 37%; 4 patients were not evaluable for response. Median PFS and OS were 1.9 months (90% CI 1.8 to 3.7) and 13.4 months (90% CI 8.2 to 27.1), respectively. The most common treatment-emergent adverse events of any grade included fatigue, pruritus, infusion-related reaction, and increases in amylase (8.6% each). Exploratory biomarker analyses in paired tumor biopsies showed an increase in intratumoral CD8 T-cell density and an upregulation of gene signatures related to interferon-γ signaling, antigen presentation, and T-cell activation with treatment without, however, clear association with efficacy endpoints.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Dual PD-1/TIM-3 inhibition was tolerable but exhibited modest antitumor activity in patients with advanced/metastatic recurrent BTC who had not received prior anti-PD-(L)1 treatment.

sec.title: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC

list-item.p: Current evidence suggests that the engagement of the galectin-9/T-cell immunoglobulin and mucin-domain containing 3 (TIM-3) pathway may impair T-cell cytotoxicity in biliary tract cancers (BTC).

This is the first clinical trial to investigate the combination of an anti-programmed cell death protein-1 (PD-1) antibody with a TIM-3-targeting antibody in patients with advanced/metastatic BTC, whose disease progressed under treatment with at least one line of systemic therapy and who had not received prior treatment with programmed death-ligand 1 inhibitors. Our study demonstrated that dual PD-1/TIM-3 inhibition was tolerable and induced immune changes in the tumor microenvironment but exhibited modest clinical activity in unselected patients with BTC.

sec.title: HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY

list-item.p: Further molecular profiling and identification of biomarkers that may predict response to TIM-3 targeting in BTC is warranted.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Biliary tract cancers (BTC) comprise intrahepatic and extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and gallbladder cancers. They account for less than 5% of all gastrointestinal malignancies and represent aggressive tumors with a poor prognosis.1 For several years, first-line standard of care treatment for patients with advanced/metastatic BTC was limited to chemotherapy with gemcitabine and cisplatin. The efficacy of chemotherapy is, however, limited with median overall survival (OS) of approximately 11 months.2 Immunotherapies and targeted therapies have recently changed the treatment of BTC. The KEYNOTE-966 and TOPAZ-1 phase III trials demonstrated improved OS with programmed cell death protein-1 (PD-1)/programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) inhibitors added to chemotherapy, establishing gemcitabine/cisplatin plus durvalumab or pembrolizumab as the first-line treatment.3 4

Despite the improvement in outcome, the activity of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) in patients with BTC remains modest, underscoring the need for the development of novel therapeutic strategies. Recent evidence suggests that T-cell immunoglobulin and mucin-domain containing 3 (TIM-3), an immune checkpoint receptor expressed by a range of different immune cells, including dysfunctional T cells, dendritic cells (DCs), macrophages, and natural killer (NK) cells—is highly expressed on T cells in gallbladder cancers, and may be a novel checkpoint target for patients with BTC.5 Both TIM-3 and its ligand galectin-9 are expressed in resectable BTC tumors with data suggesting that engagement of the galectin-9/TIM-3 pathway may impair T-cell cytotoxicity in these tumors.6

S095018 (also known as Sym023) is a human anti-TIM-3 IgG2 antibody which blocks binding of several ligands (galectin-9, phosphatidyl serine) to TIM-3, stimulating the activity of T cells, DCs, and macrophages. Sym021 is a humanized IgG1 Fc-inactivated antibody that inhibits binding of PD-1 to its ligands PD-L1 and PD-L2.7 The phase I clinical trial of single-agent Sym021 showed safety and preliminary antitumor activity in patients with advanced cancers.8 Preclinical studies demonstrated that S095018 combined with Sym021 resulted in enhanced antitumor activity. Clinical data from the phase I study of S095018 as a single agent9 or in combination with Sym02110 showed that S095018 is well tolerated both as a single agent and in combination with Sym021 with neither dose-limiting toxicities as a single agent nor maximum tolerated dose being reached for the combination. In the phase I single-agent dose-escalation study of S095018, 10 patients (43.5%) had stable disease (SD) as their best overall response (BOR), with 3 patients (13%) achieving SD that lasted more than 16 weeks. Notably, among 27 patients with advanced cancer who received S095018 in combination with Sym021 in a phase I dose-finding study, 3 patients (11.1%) achieved objective responses, including 1 patient with gallbladder carcinoma who achieved a durable complete response (CR) that lasted for 3 years. Here, we report the results from the phase Ib assessment of S095018 in combination with Sym021 in an expansion cohort of patients with advanced/metastatic recurrent biliary tract cancer who were naive to prior anti-PD-(L)1 treatment.

sec.title: Study design and patient eligibility
sec.p: This study was part of a phase Ib multicenter, open-label, non-randomized clinical trial investigating the anti-TIM-3 antibody S095018 in combination with the anti-PD-1 antibody Sym021 in patients with histologically confirmed advanced/metastatic BTC whose disease progressed on treatment with at least one line of systemic therapy, and who had not received prior treatment with PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors.11 Eligible patients were required to be ≥18 years old and diagnosed with locally advanced or metastatic biliary tract carcinoma, including adenocarcinoma of the intrahepatic and/or extrahepatic bile ducts and gallbladder carcinoma. Patients with ampullary cancers were excluded. Patients must have received and progressed on or been intolerant to first-line gemcitabine and platinum-based chemotherapy. Patients with known fibroblast growth factor receptor 2 fusion or rearrangement, or isocitrate dehydrogenase 1 mutation were excluded. Patients were required to have measurable disease according to RECIST V.1.1, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status of 0 or 1, and adequate organ function.

sec.title: Treatment
sec.p: Patients received Sym021 at a dose of 3 mg/kg followed by S095018 at a dose of 10 mg/kg via intravenous infusion. Sym021 was infused over approximately 30 min followed by a 30 min rest period before the infusion of S095018. S095018 was also infused over approximately 30 min (+10 min). The study drugs were administered once every 2 weeks, that is, on day 1 and day 15 of each 4-week (28-day) dosing cycle for up to 2 years or until unacceptable toxicity, documented disease progression, or treatment discontinuation at the discretion of the investigator or the patient. The dosing rationale is based on data from prior phase I dose escalation studies for S095018/Sym23 and Sym021.10 In particular, S095018 given alone or with the anti-PD-1 antibody Sym021 at doses ranging from 0.03 to 20 mg/kg every 2 weeks (Q2W) showed a favorable safety profile with no maximum tolerated dose identified in the phase I dose escalation study. Since no clear dose-response relationship for antitumor activity was observed, dose selection relied mainly on pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) findings: (1) PK data showing linear dose-exposure relationship observed at the recommended dose, and (2) PD data demonstrating dose-dependent increases in soluble TIM3 levels, with a plateau observed at ≥10 mg/kg, indicating sufficient and saturable target engagement. The recommended dose of Sym021 (3 mg/kg Q2W) was established based on dose-escalation data evaluating doses from 0.3 to 10 mg/kg Q2W in a phase I trial.10 This study demonstrated a dose-dependent increase in exposure, and PD data confirmed that this dose level ensures maximal PD-1 blockade. In the present study, both compounds were administered at their respective recommended doses (10 mg/kg for S095018 and 3 mg/kg for Sym021; both Q2W), as the prior dose-escalation study of TIM3 with a fixed dose of Sym021 demonstrated that the PK of one compound did not impact the other, and the combination was safe and well tolerated.

sec.title: Study assessments
sec.p: The primary objectives of this study were to evaluate the efficacy and safety/tolerability of S095018 in combination with Sym021 in patients with BTC. The overall response rate (ORR), defined as the proportion of patients with a BOR of CR or partial response (PR) as per RECIST V.1.1, was the primary efficacy endpoint. The sample size was not based on power consideration but to provide a reasonable precision of the estimation of ORR and an adequate control of the false positive and false negative rates, assuming a historical response rate of approximately 5–10%, and a target response rate of 20%. The incidence and severity of adverse events (AEs), including serious adverse events (SAEs) and AEs leading to dose interruption, dose delay or treatment discontinuation were the primary safety endpoints. Key secondary objectives/endpoints included the assessment of PK and immunogenicity, progression-free survival (PFS), disease control rate (DCR) defined as CR, PR, or SD ≥6 months, OS, as well as determination of ORR per iRECIST. PFS was defined as the time (in months) from the date of first dosing until the date of radiologic progressive disease (PD) (as defined by RECIST V.1.1) or death (by any cause in the absence of progression), whichever occurred earlier. OS was defined as the time (in months) from the date of first dosing until the date of death by any cause. The method used to estimate the median follow-up time was forward follow-up. The assessment of predictive and PD biomarkers in blood and tumor tissue were exploratory objectives of the study. Patients were evaluated for response every 8 weeks (±7 days) starting from the first dose of study treatment. AEs were assessed and graded using the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events V.5.0.

sec.title: Patient follow-up
sec.p: Per-protocol, all patients were followed up for a minimum of 30 days after the last dose of study drugs for occurrence of new-onset or resolution of ongoing (S)AEs. In addition, there was a long-term surveillance to monitor for new-onset or ongoing immune-mediated toxicities for up to 6 months after the last dose of study drug(s). Ongoing immune-mediated toxicities at the 6-month long-term FUP visit were followed at approximately 2-month intervals for up to 1 year to assess the course of the condition and to evaluate the potential reversibility of the finding. If a non-immune-mediated AE of ≥grade 2 severity that was considered possibly related, probably related, or related to study drug(s) had not resolved by the 1 month FUP evaluation, patients were assessed during the long-term FUP for safety until resolution of the event or up to 1 year, whichever came first.

sec.title: Pharmacokinetics and immunogenicity assessment
sec.p: Serum samples for PK analyses were obtained at the following time points: pre-dose, end of Sym021 infusion (EoI1), end of S095018 infusion (EoI2), and 2, 4, 8, 24, 48, and 168 hours after EoI2 on C1D1, at pre-dose, EoI1 and EoI2 on C1D15, then at pre-dose, EoI1 and EoI2 on D1 and D15 of cycle 2 and every odd cycle from cycle 3.

Free S095018 and Sym021 serum concentrations were determined by a validated TIM-3 and PD-1 target binding immunoassay using the GyroLab platform, with a lower limit of quantification of 400 ng/mL. PK analyses were conducted using non-compartmental analysis (NCA) methods. The primary PK parameters, including the area under the plasma concentration-time curve (AUC), maximum observed concentration (Cmax), time to maximum concentration, and elimination half-life (t½), were calculated. NCA was performed using PKanalix software (V.2023R1, Lixoft). Graphical representations of the data were generated using R software (V.4.2.2).

Serum samples for anti-drug (S095018) and Sym021 antibodies (ADA) were obtained at baseline (screening visit and/or C1D1), and prior to infusion throughout the treatment period on C1D15, C2D1, and then every odd cycle from C3D1 onwards. ADA samples were also collected from patients available at end-of-treatment and follow-up visits. Assessments of anti-S095018 and anti-Sym021 ADA responses were conducted at Labcorp Early Development Laboratories by detection, confirmation, and titration of S095018 and Sym021 binding ADA using, respectively, a S095018 and Sym021 ADA-specific bridging assay on the Meso Scale Discovery (MSD) platform. For the S095018 ADA bridging assay, the lower limit of detection for the positive ADA control (rabbit-anti-S095018) in the absence of drug (S095018) was 5 ng/mL. In the presence of S095018 at 100 µg/mL, the sensitivity for the positive ADA control was 100 ng/mL. For the Sym021 ADA bridging assay, the lower limit of detection for the positive ADA control (rabbit-anti-Sym021) in the absence of drug (Sym021) was 2 ng/mL. In the presence of Sym021 at 500 µg/mL, the sensitivity for the positive ADA control was 50 ng/mL.

sec.title: Biomarker assessments in blood
sec.p: Total soluble TIM-3 (sTIM-3) was measured in human serum samples with an MSD method developed by Symphogen (Ballerup, Denmark), transferred and validated at KCAS Bio (Lyon, France). Briefly, MSD plates were coated with a monoclonal anti-TIM-3 capture antibody and the plates were washed and saturated. Samples, quality control, and calibrators were pre-incubated in sample diluent containing S095018 and then loaded into the MSD plates. Then, the plates were washed and an SULFO-tagged polyclonal detection Ab with an epitope different from S095018 target epitope was added to the plate to detect total sTIM-3. After incubation and washing, a read buffer was added, before reading in the MSD SQ120 instrument. Total sTIM-3 was measured in serum in a range of 3.02 ng/mL to 487.26 ng/mL, with a precision of <14.9%.

Peripheral blood samples were collected in EDTA K2 tubes, and the plasma was stored at −20°C. The relative levels of 92 cytokines were analyzed in the frozen plasma samples at baseline and at the end of cycle 1 (EOC1) using the Olink Immuno-Oncology panel (Olink Proteomics AB, Uppsala, Sweden), which is based on the previously described proximity extension assay technology.12 To prevent batch effects, the plasma samples were randomized across the assay. Protein levels were measured in normalized protein expression (NPX) units according to the manufacturer’s recommendations.13

Plasma was centrifuged two times and stored at −20°C. Cell-free DNA was extracted from 4 to 6 mL of plasma using the QIAamp Circulating Nucleic Acid kit (Qiagen) next generation sequencing (NGS) of plasma-derived cell-free DNA was conducted using Guardant360, a clinical NGS assay that is College of American Pathologists/Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments (CAP/CLIA) accredited and US Food and Drug Administration-approved, developed by Guardant Health (Redwood City, California, USA). Single nucleotide variants and small insertions/deletions in 74 genes, copy number amplifications in 18 genes, and gene rearrangements/fusions in 6 genes were interrogated. In addition, the NGS panel has been validated for microsatellite instability (MSI) assessment.14 Germline alterations were filtered out as previously described.15 16 MSI was assessed by evaluating somatic changes in the length of repetitive sequences on the Guardant360 panel (90 evaluated loci). A sample is called “MSI-High Detected” if the number of unstable loci is above a threshold set at 6 established on 84 healthy donor samples and validated on a cohort of 1,145 archived samples.

sec.title: Biomarker assessments in tumors
sec.p: Core needle formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded biopsies were collected at baseline and at the EOC1. The samples were sent to Veracyte for multiplex immunohistochemistry (IHC) and gene expression profiling analysis (NanoString). An H&E-stained slide from each biopsy was examined by a pathologist to assess tumor cellularity and tissue quality.

For IHC analysis, the Brightplex technology, which involves a sequential chromogenic staining solution developed by Veracyte and applied using a Leica Bond RX autostainer, was used. Two Brightplex IHC panels were performed on biopsy sections: Panel 1 (TIM-3, PD-1, LAG-3, CD3, CD8, Nkp46, GrzB) and Panel 2 (CD68, DC-Lamp, TIM-3, CD86, MHC-II, CD45, pan cytokeratins) to evaluate T-cell and myeloid immune populations. Hematoxylin counterstaining (for cellular nuclei) was conducted after each staining. Coverslips were mounted with an aqueous medium, and each slide was scanned using the NanoZoomer XR at ×20 magnification. Coverslips were carefully removed from the slides using a warm water bath, and the slides were (3-amino-9-ethylcarbazole) AEC/AMEC-destained with ethanol before the antibodies were stripped with a denaturing solution. All scanned images were aligned in Halo software (Indica Labs). Regions of interest, such as tumor islets or parenchyma, stroma, and whole tumor, were selected, and phenotypes were visually verified based on expected staining. Raw data included cell counts (cells/mm²) for each phenotype in the regions of interest. Additionally, pretreatment sections were stained with the anti-PD-L1 HDX2 monoclonal antibody using the Benchmark XT Ventana auto stainer. Each sample was then analyzed by a pathologist to determine PD-L1 immune cell score, tumor cell score, tumor proportion score, and CPS (combined positive score) scores.

For the NanoString analysis, the pathologist delineated the tumor cell areas for macrodissection prior to RNA extraction. Total RNA was extracted from each sample using the RNeasy FFPE kit from Qiagen.17 The quantity and quality of the extracted RNA were assessed for quality control. Gene expression profiling was conducted using the nCounter PanCancer Immune panel, which included 30 additional targeted genes: BCL2L11, CASP2, BCAP31, TRAF1, CD82, CRADD, CTSC, CUL9, MCL1, PDCD2, RAF1, PTK2, PSMC2, CD226, CD200R1, B2M, BCAP31, TGFB3, ADORA1, ADORA3, ADORA2B, TAGAP, CIITA, NGK7, HLA-DRB1, PF_4, PROM1, REN, TSLP, IHH, and CD69. Raw count data were preprocessed using the NanoStringNorm R package.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Clinical efficacy endpoints were analyzed using point estimates and CIs. Median PFS and OS were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method. CIs for median PFS and OS were based on the log–log transformation. Follow-up time in months was defined as the duration from the date of first Investigational Medicinal Product (IMP) dose to the date of study discontinuation.

Multiplex IHC analysis, Olink cytokine measurements, and NanoString Pancancer immune transcriptomic profiling were conducted. Data were expressed in log2(density) for IHC, NPX for cytokines, and log2(normalized count) for transcriptomic profiling, respectively. NanoString signature scores were calculated using the mean expression of gene sets. Biomarker expression was visualized using line plots for each subject with paired tumor biopsies. Subsequently, statistical tests were performed on changes between EOC1 and screening. Biomarker data were also explored in relation to BOR. Partial responders and patients with SD for more than 6 months were classified as responders. The relationship between changes in biomarkers from baseline and response status was analyzed. For all analyses, the Limma model was used for cytokine and NanoString measurements at the gene level. Wilcoxon tests were performed for NanoString signature scores and multiplex IHC data. Statistical significance was set at a p value threshold of 0.05, with an absolute fold change greater than 1.3 considered significant. All analyses were conducted using R software V.4.4.1 (2024–06-14).

sec.title: Results
sec.p: As of September 25, 2024, a total of 35 patients with recurrent biliary tract cancer (34 with stage 4 disease, 1 unknown) were treated with S095018 in combination with Sym021. 34 patients had cholangiocarcinoma, and 1 patient had gallbladder adenocarcinoma. Median age was 66 years (range 47–76 years). ECOG performance status was 0 for 13 patients (37.1%) and 1 for 22 patients (62.9%). All patients were naive to prior PD-1/L1 inhibitors. All patients had received prior systemic treatment. 13 patients (37.1%) had received 1 prior antineoplastic systemic treatment, and 22 patients (62.9%) had received ≥2 prior treatments. The median duration of exposure to study treatment was 3.2 months (range 0.5–25 months). As of September 25, 2024, no patient remained on study treatment; 26 patients (74.3%) discontinued treatment due to documented (radiologically confirmed) disease progression and 5 patients (14.3%) due to clinical progression. sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p: Median follow-up was 9.2 months. Among the 35 treated patients, 31 (88.6%) patients were evaluable for response using RECIST V.1.1. The ORR was 5.7% (95% CI 1.6% to 18.6%) both by RECIST V.1.1 and iRECIST, with PR reported in two patients. SD was reported in 11 patients (31.4%), with 5 patients having SD for ≥6 months. Four patients were not evaluable for BOR assessment. Three patients did not have any post-baseline assessment. The fourth patient had one scan showing SD; however, since the SD was observed very early and did not persist for the required duration (≥8 weeks), the BOR was not considered evaluable. The DCR at 16 weeks, 24 weeks, and 12 months was 28.6% (95% CI 16.3% to 45.1%), 22.9% (95% CI 12.1% to 39.0%), and 8.6%, respectively (95% CI 3.0% to 22.4%). The waterfall plot for best percentage change from baseline per RECIST V.1.1 is shown in figure 1A. The swimmer plot and spider plot with the duration of response are shown in figure 1B and C. The duration of response for the two patients with PR was 23.6 and 3.5 months. The median PFS per RECIST V.1.1 was 1.9 months (95% CI 1.8 to 3.5) (figure 2A). The median OS was 13.4 months (95% CI 5.7 to 19.4) (figure 2B). The OS CI is relatively wide given the limited sample size and number of events observed. Two patients were censored for PFS. This included one patient who was still followed without radiologic PD or death as of the cut-off date, and one patient without adequate baseline or post-baseline assessment. 16 patients were censored for OS. All 16 patients were still followed without a death event as of the cut-off date (online supplemental Table 5). CT images from the two patients achieving PR are presented in online supplemental figure 1.

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: 33 patients (94.3%) experienced at least one treatment-emergent AE of any grade. The most frequently reported AEs regardless of relationship to study treatment were fatigue (seven patients, 20%), abdominal pain (seven patients, 20%), anemia (six patients, 17.1%), and blood creatinine increase (six patients, 17.1%) (online supplemental table 1). AEs of any grade suspected to be related to study treatment were reported in 24 patients (68.6%). The most frequent treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) of any grade suspected to be related to the study were fatigue (three patients, 8.6%), infusion-related reaction (three patients, 8.6%), pruritus (three patients, 8.6%), and increased amylase (three patients, 8.6%). Increased blood alkaline phosphatase, hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism, increased lipase, and myalgia related to study treatment were reported in two patients each (5.7%) (table 2). Most TRAEs were grade 1–2. Grade 3 TRAEs were reported in four patients (11.4%). These included increased amylase (n=1), increased lipase (n=1), increased aspartate aminotransferase (n=1), lymphopenia (n=1), anemia (n=1), colitis (n=1), and immune-mediated cytopenia (n=1). The patient with grade 3 colitis and immune-mediated cytopenia discontinued treatment due to drug toxicity. The event of grade 3 colitis resolved after treatment with corticosteroids per institutional guidelines. Three SAEs suspected to be treatment-related (anemia, colitis, and immune-mediated cytopenia) were reported in 1 (2.9%) patient. 50% of the patients who developed immune-related adverse events in this study required steroid treatment during study participation.

sec.title: Pharmacokinetic and immunogenicity
sec.p: PK parameters for S095018 and Sym021 are presented in the online supplemental table 2 and online supplemental table 3, respectively. The PK profiles were linear.

The mean S095018 exposure AUCtau was 36,883.2±11,837.5 hour/µg/mL and the Cmax was 279.2±132.6 µg/mL (figure 3A). The mean t½ of S095018 was 13.0 days (±8.4 days). No significant effect of Sym021 on S095018 PK was observed. Trough concentration assessment revealed drug accumulation across multiple dosing cycles with steady state reached after week 13 (figure 3B).

Immunogenicity assessment in 33 evaluable patients showed no evidence of treatment-induced ADAs against S095018. ADAs against Sym021 were detected in four patients at baseline with two patients having measurable ADA at the last study visit.

sec.p: To study the PD effects of S095018 in combination with Sym021, we performed extensive immune profiling by multiplex IHC as well as a transcriptomic analysis using NanoString pancancer immune panel on formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tumor biopsies. NanoString analysis was performed in tumor samples from 19 evaluable patients with paired biopsies. IHC was performed on tumor samples from 21 evaluable patients. Out of the 19 patients with paired NanoString data, only 18 were evaluable for multiplex IHC assessment. Biomarkers were assessed at baseline and at the EOC1 using paired tumor biopsies from the same location. Analysis of paired tumor biopsies from 19 evaluable patients showed that the combination treatment led to an increase in the density of CD8+T cells in the tumor microenvironment (TME) (p<0.05), as well as an upregulation of NanoString gene signatures related to antigen processing and cytotoxicity (figure 4B, online supplemental figure 2). T-cell recruitment and proliferation in the TME (p<0.05) was associated with an upregulation of immune checkpoint molecules (LAG-3, TIGIT, CD27, HAVCR2, CTLA-4) (p<0.005) (figure 4C). In addition, a significant upregulation of cytotoxic and NK cell-related genes (GZMA, NKG7) was detected (figure 4C).

NanoString transcriptomic data identified several genes (C8B, CCL16, MASP2, ARG1, MPPED1, CLU) upregulated in patients with clinical benefit (eg, PR or SD ≥6 months) and one gene downregulated (MAGEA3) (online supplemental Figure 4A), (online supplemental Figure 4F). In addition, a non-significant trend towards upregulation of the complement pathway in responders was also observed (online supplemental Figure 4D). Multiplex IHC analyses on tumor biopsies did not reveal significant differences in T-cell density and T-cell activation associated with response (online supplemental Figure 4C), (online supplemental Figure 4G). In plasma samples from 18 evaluable patients, a trend towards downregulation of several cytokines, including EGF, CXCL5, CD40L, FGF2, and CCL17 was noticed in patients with clinical benefit (online supplemental Figure 4B), (online supplemental Figure 4E). However, none of these associations remained statistically significant after correction for multiple testing (FDR threshold 0.2).

Multiplex IHC and transcriptomic profiling of two patients (one patient with PR and one patient with SD that lasted more than 6 months) demonstrated high levels of immune infiltrates (mainly T cells and macrophages), as well as a high score of tumor inflammation signature and strong CXCL13 mRNA expression (figure 4D). Among tumor samples evaluable for PD-L1, tumors from 13 patients (43.3%) had a CPS ≥1% (table 1). Tumor samples from the three patients with the highest decrease in tumor size (two PR, one SD) had high levels of PD-L1 expression with CPS >25 (figure 4D). Investigation of MSI (Microsatelitte Instable High) status using Guardant Health 360 targeted panel in plasma showed no Microsatelitte instable high MSI-H tumors (online supplemental Table 6). Tumor mutation status in 18 patient samples is presented in the online supplemental figure 3.

The neutrophil/lymphocyte ratio at baseline was assessed for all patients. The mean neutrophil/lymphocyte ratio was 5.1 (SD 4.27) for the entire patient population. The mean neutrophil/lymphocyte ratio was 7.79 for the 7 patients with clinical benefit (eg, patients with CR, PR or SD ≥6 months), compared with 4.43 for the 28 patients without clinical benefit (online supplemental Table 6).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Biliary tract cancer presents substantial therapeutic challenges due to its aggressive nature and poor prognosis. To our knowledge, this study is the first clinical trial to investigate the combination of an anti-PD-1 antibody with a TIM-3-targeting antibody in patients with BTC. Evidence suggests that BTC promotes an immunosuppressive TME with upregulated TIM-3 expression possibly contributing to immune evasion mechanisms.18 19 Studies have demonstrated that PD-1 and TIM-3 co-expression on tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes in cholangiocarcinoma correlates with diminished antitumor immunity and shorter OS.5 These data highlight the potential of TIM-3 as a compelling therapeutic target. Our rationale to test the combination of anti-TIM-3 S095018 and anti-PD-1 Sym021 in BTC was also supported by evidence from a phase I dose-finding study, which demonstrated a durable CR in a patient with gallbladder carcinoma who was treated with S095018 in combination with Sym021.10

The data from our cohort of 35 patients with advanced/metastatic recurrent BTC who had not received prior anti-PD-(L)1 treatment suggest that the combination of S095018 and Sym021 is tolerable and exhibits modest antitumor activity in this unselected patient population. However, given that these patients were naive to immunotherapy, the contribution of adding anti-TIM-3 to anti-PD-1 remains unclear. ORR was 5.7% and DCR at 16 weeks and 24 weeks were approximately 29% and 23%, respectively, while median PFS and OS were 1.9 months and 13.4 months, respectively. In the phase II KEYNOTE-158 study, pembrolizumab was administered as a single agent to patients with previously treated advanced cholangiocarcinoma, the ORR was 5.8% with a median PFS of 2.0 months, comparable to our study. However, median OS was only 7.4 months in KEYNOTE-158.20 In KEYNOTE-028, only patients with PD-L1-positive tumors (CPS ≥1) were enrolled, and while ORR was numerically higher compared with KEYNOTE-158 (13%), median PFS and OS were comparable (1.8 months and 5.7 months, respectively).20 A cohort of 30 Japanese patients with recurrent BTC refractory to gemcitabine-based chemotherapy in a phase I study of nivolumab monotherapy showed an ORR of 3% with median PFS and OS of 1.4 and 5.2 months, respectively,21 while a study of single-agent durvalumab in 42 patients from Asia with advanced BTC showed an ORR of 4.8% with median PFS and median OS of 1.5 and 8.1 months, respectively.22 A phase I study evaluating the anti-PD-1 antibody toripalimab in 42 patients with advanced/refractory cholangiocarcinoma showed similar ORR (4.8%) with median PFS of 2.1 months.23 Our data show a numerically higher OS (13.4 months) compared with early phase studies of single-agent PD-1 inhibitors (6–8 months). However, comparable OS was reported in a phase II clinical trial of single-agent nivolumab (14.24 months)24; in this study of unselected patients with BTC, ORR was 11% alongside a median PFS of 3.68 months. A notable difference between this study and our trial is that 59% of patients in the nivolumab study had intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, while 31% had gallbladder cancer. In comparison, only 1 patient in our study had gallbladder carcinoma (2.8%), while 10 patients (28.6%) had reported intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma. Potential differences in other key patient characteristics, such as PD-L1 status and number of prior systemic treatments may affect the clinical outcomes of ICIs. In regard to PD-L1 status, the proportion of patients with PD-L1-positive BTC (eg, PD-L1 ≥1%) was 58.7% in KEYNOTE-158, 100% in KEYNOTE-028, 45.2% in the durvalumab study, and 43% in the nivolumab phase II study, while 43.3% of the evaluable tumor samples in our study (3/30) had PD-L1 ≥1%. Of note, PD-L1 status in our trial was assessed in tumor biopsies collected at baseline (eg, post chemotherapy). In addition, 62.9% of patients in our trial had received ≥2 prior systemic treatments; this was the case for 58.7% of patients in KEYNOTE-158, 87.5% in KEYNOTE-028, 83.2% of patients in the durvalumab study, and 50% in the nivolumab phase II study. Immunotherapy combinations have also been tested in patients with BTC. The combination of durvalumab with anti-cytotoxic T-lymphocyte associated protein 4 (CTLA-4) tremelimumab in 65 patients with BTC showed a response rate of 10.8% and median PFS and OS of 1.6 and 10.1 months, respectively.22 Similarly, the combination of nivolumab and ipilimumab in the CA209-538 study demonstrated numerically higher ORR (23%) with comparable median PFS (2.9 months) and numerically lower median OS (5.7 months).25 Notably, the anti-PD-(L)1/CTLA-4 combinations were associated with higher incidences of grade ≥3 TRAEs (23.1% for durvalumab/tremelimumab22; 20% for nivolumab/ipilimumab compared with our study (11.4%). sec.p: Biomarker assessment in our trial showed increases in immune cell densities including CD8+T cell and NK cell densities after treatment. Moreover, upregulation of pathways related to cytotoxicity was detected following dual TIM-3/PD-1 inhibition. Consistent with the literature, activation of T cells and NK cells led to upregulation of interferon (IFN)-γ26 as well as strong expression of IFN-γ-induced inflammatory chemokines such as CXCL9, CXCL10, and CXCL11, mainly secreted by macrophages and dendritic cells.27 Transcriptomic data revealed that the combination of S095018 and Sym021 drives significant functional changes in the myeloid compartment with a strong upregulation of antigen processing/presentation related genes. Together, these biomarker data indicate that dual TIM-3/PD-1 inhibition induces immune changes in the TME including functional changes in the myeloid compartment with increased antigen presentation, recruitment, and activation of cytotoxic T cells and NK cells. While our study provides evidence for immune activation in the TME, the relative contribution of TIM-3 blockade needs to be further explored as anti-PD-1 treatment alone has also been associated with increases in T-cell inflamed signatures.26 28

Despite PD biomarker responses, clinical activity was limited in our trial. Our biomarker data identified genes upregulated in patients with clinical benefit, while IHC did not show significant differences in T-cell density or activation associated with response. One key limitation of our exploratory biomarker analysis is the limited sample size of patients with clinical benefit in the population of the biomarker evaluable patients (one patient with PR, three patients with SD ≥6 months). In other studies, immunotherapy PD effects, such as increases of immune-cell subsets, upregulation of immune checkpoint genes and specific immune-related transcriptional networks correlated with tumor shrinkage.29 In melanoma, for example, an early increase in CD8+ T cells within <2 months of treatment was seen primarily in responders.30 The correlation between PD effects and clinical response has been mainly observed in more immunogenic tumor types. However, in less immunogenic malignancies, non-productive T-cell responses and IFN-γ signaling activation can be induced by immune checkpoint inhibitors,31 and as a result, the PD effects may not correlate with clinical response. Reasons for immunotherapy resistance and discordance between immunotherapy PD effects and clinical activity may include T-cell exhaustion, insensibility and dysfunctionality or suppression by other mechanisms in the TME, such as regulatory T cells or suppressive cytokines.32 In BTC, monocytes expressing high levels of immunosuppressive cytokines can induce T-cell paralysis leading to immunotherapy resistance,33 while the desmoplastic stroma of BTC may also limit the efficacy of immunotherapies.34

The patients in our study received immunotherapy combination after their disease progressed under treatment with at least one line of systemic therapy. Approximately two-thirds of the patients had received two or more lines of prior systemic treatment. Heavily pretreated patients may respond less to immunotherapy as their immunity may be more deteriorated after myeloablative chemotherapies. Moreover, chemoimmunotherapy combination has been shown to provide promising results in various studies as chemotherapy may debulk larger tumor masses, induce antitumor immunity by stimulating antigen presentation and by targeting immunosuppressive immune cells, and activate T cell and NK cell responses.35 In biliary tract cancer, early addition of immunotherapy to chemotherapy improves outcomes compared with chemotherapy alone.3 4 36 Together, this may suggest that adding novel immune-therapeutics to front line anti-PD-(L)1 in combination with chemotherapy may have higher potential for better treatment outcomes, a hypothesis that warrants further investigation.

A critical challenge and area of research includes the identification of patient groups that are more likely to benefit from immunotherapy combinations. In regard to predictive biomarkers of response, baseline biomarker data suggest that tumors from patients with higher tumor size reductions display immune hot characteristics. Notably, consistent with data from other trials of ICIs in BTC, both patients with a PR in our study showed high baseline PD-L1 expression. Due to the limited number of responders, no statistical correlation between on-treatment biomarkers and clinical outcomes was performed.

In conclusion, the combination of Sym021 and S095018 in patients with advanced/metastatic BTC who have not received prior ICI treatment demonstrated modest clinical activity as well as induction of immune changes in the TME. Key limitations of our study include the small sample cohort and the lack of a randomized single-agent anti-PD-1 comparator arm. Larger randomized clinical trials will be needed to better understand the role of TIM-3 as a therapeutic target in BTC. Notably, despite PD findings of immune activation, the clinical results of our trial do not provide clear evidence supporting a contribution of TIM-3 inhibitors to anti-PD-1 therapy in unselected patients with BTC. Extensive molecular profiling and identification of biomarkers that may predict response to TIM-3 targeting in BTC is warranted prior to further exploration of S095018 immunotherapy combinations with or without chemotherapy in selected patient populations.
